metadata.title: Twenty Seconds to Decide.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_bella) — per-beat mp3 durations are MEASURED, never estimated
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Portuguese (Ola) — one of the short forms the HAI persona's word budget allows. Ep. 03 used Hej, Ep. 04 Ciao; no language repeats within the series.
metadata.purpose: Ep. 05 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, built from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 05 (Finding 'the needle' — AI flagging rare fast radio bursts in radio telescope data). Per the series notes in ideas.md, Ep. 01 already established the data-volume premise, so this episode does not re-argue it; the volume beat exists only to set up the thing that is actually new here — that the data cannot be kept.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 is the ONE accent and marks exactly one focal event per beat: the dispersion curve, the flagged candidate in the haystack, the trigger, the deletion. Dynamic spectra are ink-on-white plots framed on the cream page, the way a figure sits in a paper — deliberately unlike Ep. 04's dark photographic plates.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Ep. 03 (gravitational waves) ended on out-of-distribution failure: a classifier cannot name a class it has never seen. Ep. 04 (galaxy classification) ended on the crowd ceiling: the model predicts what people would say. Ep. 05 ends somewhere neither of those goes — the decision is IRREVERSIBLE. The rejected data is overwritten, so a false negative can never be audited, and every other method in this series can be re-run on stored data while this one cannot. The simulated-positives design decision (B08) is deliberately framed as a design tell rather than as the failure, so it does not become Ep. 03's punchline a second time.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, with RESULT lines), B11 (verdict artifact), B12 (handoff), B13 (title outro). Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py) in the Claude fidelity palette. All dynamic spectra are SYNTHETIC, generated by assets/gen_frb.py from the dispersion law, and captioned as synthetic wherever a viewer could mistake them for data. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the same GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03's BUILD-LOG.

beats.narration_text: A fast radio burst lasts a few thousandths of a second, and the telescope cannot keep the data it arrives in. So something has to decide, within about twenty seconds, whether tonight's sky was worth saving.

show.event: cream page; IRREDUCIBLY HUMAN eyebrow, then the serif segment title Twenty Seconds to Decide
spark + greeting Ola, HAI settles above the composer card
the ask types itself into the composer; send button arms when it lands
terracotta running indicator: the buffer is filling…
three result lines stagger in — method, accuracy, limit. The ask lands ANSWERED.

props.command: Fast radio bursts last milliseconds and the raw data is too big to store. What is the actual method for catching one in real time, how good is it, and what happens to everything it rejects?
output: method — dedisperse over a bank of trial DMs, then a CNN on two images
accuracy — >99.5% recall; false positives cut from ~10^5/day to a few
limit — what it rejects is overwritten, so a miss cannot be audited

beats.narration_text: I am Om Mali, and this is Humanitarians AI. Every method in this series so far could be re-run on stored data. This one cannot. That single fact changes what the machine is for.

show.event: top-left kicker: AI IN ASTRONOMY & SPACE SCIENCE · EP. 05
the name OM MALI draws on large, centre-left, terracotta hairline sweeping under it
role line fades in beneath: Humanitarians AI · presenter
the right panel sets two rows: 'every other method: re-run it' with a loop glyph, then 'this one: decide now' with a one-way arrow in the accented token
@HumanitariansAI wordmark bug settles bottom-right, inside title-safe

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. Space stretches a radio burst so its low frequencies arrive last, which gives you a shape to search for. A telescope finds far too many candidates, almost all of them from Earth. A network sorts them in real time, and whatever it rejects is deleted.

show.event: eyebrow: THE WHOLE IDEA, IN ONE BREATH
line 1 sets: 'space gives it a shape' — one synthetic waterfall appears left with its dispersion curve
line 2 sets: 'almost all of it is us' — the single plot is joined by a dense sheet of candidates, one of them terracotta
line 3 sets: 'a network sorts it in real time' — a thin gate glyph slides across the sheet
the closing line lands: WHAT IT REJECTS IS DELETED, terracotta rule under it

beats.narration_text: Start with the shape. A burst leaves its source at every frequency at once, then crosses thousands of light years of thin plasma, which slows the low frequencies more than the high ones. By the time it arrives it is a curve. The steeper the curve, the more space it crossed.

show.event: title: WHAT SPACE DOES TO A BURST; an empty frequency-time axis draws, high frequency at the top
at the source, a vertical line: every frequency leaves at the same instant
a plasma band slides across and the line shears into a curve, low frequencies lagging
the real synthetic waterfall replaces the schematic, the same curve now in data
three panels at DM 200, 500 and 900 on one shared time axis; the slope visibly steepens
footer: the delay goes as frequency to the minus two · dispersion measure sets the slope

beats.narration_text: Now the volume. CHIME takes in about one and a half petabytes a day, and its search computes one hundred billion signal to noise values every second. That produces something like a hundred thousand candidates a day. Almost none of them are astronomical.

show.event: title: THE HAYSTACK; a dense sheet of candidate thumbnails fills the left of the stage
right column, figure one: 1.5 PB per day, cited
figure two: 10^11 signal-to-noise values per second
figure three: ~100,000 candidates per day, the number landing in the accented token
on the sheet, exactly one tile is ringed terracotta — the only astronomical one
closing line: one of these is from space

beats.narration_text: Because most of what a radio telescope sees is us. Phones, satellites, power lines, arriving at every frequency at once, with no curve. And then the famous case at Parkes. For years a signal called a peryton looked almost right. It was the observatory microwave oven, opened before its timer finished.

show.event: title: MOST OF IT IS US; three framed impostor plots draw across the stage
plot 1 fills: a vertical broadband spike, label ZERO DISPERSION, sub 'arrives at every frequency at once'
plot 2 fills: horizontal stripes, label NARROWBAND, sub 'a transmitter, always on'
plot 3 fills: blobs, label PATCHY, sub 'bursty, band-limited, no sweep'
a reference curve is overlaid on plot 1 in terracotta — the shape the search wants, and the shape this candidate lacks
a callout card sets: PARKES · the peryton was the staff microwave oven, opened before the timer finished
closing line: the false positives are man-made

beats.narration_text: So here is the method, and the clock is part of it. Raw voltages land in a ring buffer that holds about thirty five seconds. The search dedisperses the stream over a bank of trial delays. Anything that peaks becomes a candidate, rendered as two pictures. A network judges them. Yes writes a hundred milliseconds to disk. No lets the buffer move on.

show.event: title: THE LOOP, AND THE CLOCK; a ring buffer draws as a circle at the left, marked 35.5 s
station 1 lights: BUFFER — the ring fills and its write head advances
station 2 lights: DEDISPERSE — a fan of trial delay curves is laid over the stream
station 3 lights: CANDIDATE — one trial peaks and becomes two small pictures
station 4 lights: CLASSIFY — a layered network glyph reads both pictures
station 5 lights: KEEP — on a yes, a 100 ms slice is written to disk in terracotta
a grey return arc runs from station 5 back to the ring, labelled 'on a no, the buffer overwrites'

beats.narration_text: Run one through it. The sweep peaks at a trial value near five hundred, and that becomes the first picture. The second is signal strength against trial delay, where a real burst closes to a point and local interference never does. The network sees both, and calls it.

show.event: the five stations persist as a thin rail across the top; a terracotta marker sits at CANDIDATE
picture one appears: the frequency-time waterfall with its curve, labelled 'what it looks like'
picture two appears beside it: the DM-time plane, the bowtie closing to a point, labelled 'where it focuses'
the same two pictures for a zero-dispersion impostor are stacked beneath, its bowtie apex pinned to the bottom edge and never closing
both pairs feed one network glyph; the marker slides to CLASSIFY
the verdict lands: BURST for the top pair, in terracotta; REJECT for the bottom

beats.narration_text: Now the decision that makes this trainable at all. There are not enough real bursts to learn from. So the positives are simulated, injected into real telescope noise, and the negatives are real interference recorded at the dish. The fakes teach it what to want. The real ones teach it what to refuse.

show.event: title: FAKE POSITIVES, REAL NEGATIVES; the stage splits into two labelled columns
left column: SIMULATED — a synthetic curve is generated and injected into a panel of real noise; label 'the positives'
right column: RECORDED — three real interference plots stack up; label 'the negatives'
both columns feed one training block, ringed terracotta
two lines set beneath: the fakes teach it what to want / the real ones teach it what to refuse
footer cite: FETCH · trained on simulated FRBs and real RFI · Agarwal et al. 2020

beats.narration_text: The numbers. Published classifiers reach better than ninety nine and a half percent recall, and cut the false positives from about a hundred thousand a day down to a handful. CHIME's first catalogue held five hundred and thirty six bursts, sixty two of them repeats.

show.event: title: WHAT IT ACTUALLY DELIVERS
left: a recall arc fills past 99.5%, cited Agarwal et al. 2020
centre: a funnel collapses from ~100,000 candidates a day to a few, the survivors in terracotta, cited
right: the counter runs to 536 bursts, with 62 from 18 repeating sources called out beneath
footer cite: CHIME/FRB Catalog 1, 400 to 800 MHz, July 2018 to July 2019

beats.narration_text: Now the part that decides whether you trust it. Two limits. The positives were simulated, so the pipeline is sharpest on bursts that look like the ones somebody thought to simulate. And the rejections are not archived, they are overwritten. Every other method in this series can be re-run on last year's data. This one cannot.

show.event: title: TWO LIMITS; the stage splits into two panels
left panel: a cloud of simulated shapes with a sharp boundary drawn around them; one odd burst sits outside the boundary, unflagged
the boundary is labelled 'what somebody thought to simulate'
right panel: the ring buffer again, its write head passing a rejected candidate; the candidate greys out and is struck
a one-way arrow labelled NO RE-RUN, in terracotta; beneath it, a struck loop glyph
closing line: a miss here cannot be audited

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Dispersion gives you a shape to search for. The haystack is a hundred thousand candidates a day, almost all of it interference from Earth. A network trained on simulated bursts and real noise does the triage in about twenty seconds. And what it rejects is gone.

show.event: the artifact page scales up on the cream stage, spark + title bar
four numbered recap lines stagger in, one per spoken clause

props.artifactTitle: Twenty Seconds to Decide — one page
props.artifactHeading: The method, and what it costs
artifactLines: The physics hands you a searchable shape: low frequencies arrive last, so a real burst is a curve.
The haystack is ~100,000 candidates a day from ~1.5 PB, and almost all of it is interference from Earth.
The method: dedisperse over a bank of trial DMs, render two images per candidate, let a CNN judge both.
The cost: the buffer holds ~35 s, so a rejection is overwritten — a miss here can never be audited.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this one. I have a real time detector that must discard most of its input, because storing everything is impossible. Help me choose an operating threshold when false negatives are unrecoverable and false positives are merely expensive, design a way to audit what the detector threw away, and decide what small fraction of raw input to keep at random as a control. Then grade it on three things. A named cost for a miss. A way to measure what you lost. And a random sample kept.

the suggested prompt types itself into the composer while the voice reads it verbatim
terracotta running line: paste this into Claude…
the three-item rubric staggers in as output lines, one per spoken grading criterion

grade it: does it propose a way to MEASURE what you lost
